question.problem: At which points on the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2y \\  & =\frac{2y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{2y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=0 \\ \frac{2y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=0$ while the second equation gives $y=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2})=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$
